html:
A microprocessor is a whole computer processor on a single chip. The first one sold commercially was the Intel 4004, released by Intel in California in 1971.

It came from an order by Busicom, a Japanese company that wanted chips for a desk calculator. Intel's Ted Hoff proposed one general purpose chip that could be programmed instead of many special ones. Federico Faggin led the design, with Stanley Mazor and Busicom's Masatoshi Shima. The 4004 held about 2,300 transistors and was about as powerful as the room sized ENIAC computer of 1946.

It built on the integrated circuit of the late 1950s, which had put many transistors on one slice of silicon.

Faster chips followed quickly. The Intel 8080 (1974) ran the Altair, the first hit hobby computer, and the 8086 (1978) began the family of chips still used in most personal computers. Cheap microprocessors made the personal computer possible, including the machines of Apple, and today they run everything from phones to cars and washing machines. They are the reason Silicon Valley got its name.
